source.title: White Paper Assistance: A Step Forward Beyond the Shortcut Learning
source.authors: Xuan Cheng; Tian-Shu Xie; Xiaomin Wang; Jiali Deng; Ming-Hui Liu; Meilin Liu

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Figure values are garbled in places, but the tables and prose contain usable results.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether White Paper Assistance changes shortcut reliance and held-out performance in image-classification settings, extending the natural-label generalization topic to synthetic shortcut data, benchmark datasets, imbalanced data, and corruptions.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper's own training, intervention, and evaluation results about shortcut reliance and generalization. Cited prior-work results are not included. Figure-only hyperparameter results are omitted because the supplied figure text does not reliably preserve its values.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates White Paper Assistance, shortcut reliance, classification accuracy and corruption robustness. None of its experiments tests V1–V8. Natural-label interpolation alone does not test V1; parameter changes alone do not test V7. Its method comparisons do not constitute a new-setting test of any listed version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that WP alleviates shortcut reliance and improves classification and corruption robustness across their tested settings, while acknowledging that its mechanism remains insufficiently explained and white paper may not be optimal. Benchmark accuracy gains alone do not independently establish shortcut removal.
record.recipe_differences: Adds a white-paper training intervention that regularizes the model toward uniform outputs on an out-of-class input; the paper does not test the catalog's original interventions or measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that changing the assistance input among white paper, Gaussian noise, ice-cream images, and CIFAR-10 changes performance; it also describes performance varying with assistance probability P, strength λ, and repetition count M, though numerical values for P and λ plots are not reliably readable in the supplied text.

fits_no_version.finding: WP raises shortcut-conflict accuracy from 39.95% to 46.88%, and from 25.55% to 29.77% with the alternative shortcut class.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: White Paper Assistance can improve resistance to an intentionally added image-classification shortcut.

fits_no_version.finding: WP lowers reported classification error across tested architectures, datasets, long-tailed settings and combinations with augmentation or loss methods.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: White Paper Assistance can improve held-out classification performance in the tested training recipes.

fits_no_version.finding: WP reduces mean corruption error from 78.32% to 75.87%, with lower average error for every reported corruption type.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: White Paper Assistance can improve robustness to common corruptions on tiny-ImageNet-C.

fits_no_version.finding: White paper outperforms the tested alternative assistance inputs; head substitutions attribute immediate accuracy disruption primarily to the convolutional portion.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Assistance-input choice affects WP performance, and white-paper training can temporarily disrupt accuracy through changes to convolutional representations.

record.problems: The paper's central explanation of why white paper works is acknowledged as not fully explicable. Several figure-only results and parameter sweeps cannot be recovered from the supplied text. The synthetic shortcut experiment uses one synthetic cue and selected datasets; claims about general applicability extend beyond those specific tests.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted to meet the 60-row limit. Figure 2 values are retained as figure-only rows because the text explicitly describes their comparative result, but exact values are unavailable. Figure 9 hyperparameter sweep values and Figure 6 repetition sweep are not included because the supplied text does not state exact numerical values for each condition.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization under the same architecture and recipe.
Test-error changes with width beyond the zero-training-error threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under specified tuning conditions.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Adding or removing dropout, its dependence on training-set size, and joint removal with weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness versus generalization gaps and comparative ranking against other measures.
Removing memorized examples versus removing equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: All row links remain none. Their cannot_determine states concern V1–V8, not whether WP's reported improvements occurred. T6 applies because the study neither tests nor operationally uses a listed claim version; broad discussion of generalization does not make it T3 or T4.

versions.untested_parts: Does not train on fixed random labels or compare random-label and natural-label generalization.
No width sweep or interpolation-threshold analysis.
Does not compare convolutional networks with fully connected networks.
No magnitude-aware sharpness or other generalization-measure ranking.
Does not remove memorized examples and retrain.
